title: Do Students Still Need to Learn Math? Jensen Huang Says Maybe Not.
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Starting from Jensen Huang's remark that forgetting basic math may not matter, Bauschard argues educators should take the question seriously rather than scoff. His claim is that the familiar academic core was never rigorously justified for students with very different futures, and AI makes the trade-offs sharper. He rejects the two standard defenses, that a subject is valuable and that it teaches students to think, because every course consumes time students could spend elsewhere and many activities, from debate to robotics, also build thinking. He applies the same test to his own field, debate, and admits he still has to make that case. He accepts that students need knowledge to judge AI output, but insists each requirement be re-defended in terms of foundations, depth and practice. His closing line is that 'all the same stuff still has to be taught' is an assumption that needs an argument.
points: Explaining why a subject has value does not settle the curriculum, because every required course displaces something else a student could learn.
The claim that a subject 'teaches students to think' is too cheap, since debate, robotics and other activities do so too, and each approach must show what thinking it develops and how well.
Curriculum uniformity served a different era; if students need different things, we should ask how much common preparation they need before they diverge.
Students still need knowledge to evaluate AI reasoning, but which knowledge, at what depth, is the open question educators owe an answer to.
Neither AI's ability to do a task nor tradition alone justifies dropping or keeping it; both sides owe an explicit argument.
quotes: We have never designed a mass education system for a world where valuable cognition is not the exclusive domain of humans. We should be willing to admit that we don’t yet know exactly what and how students will need to learn to succeed in this world.

I’m not arguing that nothing in the existing curriculum matters. I’m arguing that everything needs to be (re)-defended as not only valuable but more valuable than other things students could learn in a world where advanced cognition is also artificial.
But students cannot learn everything. Even the supposedly ideal student, taking every advanced class and barely sleeping, learns only a tiny fraction of what there is to know in the world.
Every required course uses time that students could spend learning something else.

We need to explain the relevance of content in an AI world and what kind of thinking a particular teaching approach develops, how well it develops it, and whether students can use it beyond the assignment.

Of course, students need knowledge to think well. You cannot evaluate an AI’s mathematical reasoning if you understand nothing about mathematics, but that begs the question of what we want them to know in the first place.
Huang may be wrong about which skills we can afford to lose. Educators should make the case.
All the same stuff still has to be taught” is an assumption. It needs an argument.
